# Open redirect destination control

## Applicability and prerequisites

An assigned redirect, return URL or browser navigation input selects a destination. Establish the allowed destination policy and whether the feature intentionally supports arbitrary external navigation. Use controlled harmless destination URLs and stop before following to any unapproved location. Capture HTTP redirect chains and browser navigation where relevant; equivalent tooling is acceptable. Authentication codes, tokens and user data must not be sent to the receiver.

Choose only the assigned branch and obey the operation's scope, identities, rate and state-change constraints. Missing prerequisites stay explicit; a lookup signal is not proof. Equivalent available tools may replace named capabilities.

## Reconnaissance

1. Inspect the assigned return/next/location input and identify server-side Location redirects, client-side navigation or displayed links. A string echoed in a page or error does not establish navigation.
"}, {"id": 3, "text": "2. Record expected same-origin/path/partner restrictions, canonical scheme/host/port and any confirmation page. Identify whether a security workflow relies on this redirect rather than assuming phishing or token disclosure from an external link.

## Hypothesis generation

1. From recorded navigation design an allowed baseline and one controlled disallowed destination, varying only the destination interpretation. Include a nonexistent/inert input and a similarly shaped allowed destination as controls.
2. Plan a small context-justified set of URL representations such as absolute versus network-path reference, encoded delimiter or userinfo ambiguity. Define the final browser-parsed origin; do not assume a substring or visual hostname is the authority.
3. Specify whether the outcome is an HTTP redirect, a JavaScript navigation or a legitimate external link. No requests or browser navigation occur in hypothesis generation, and an unapproved token-leak chain remains outside this test.

## Vulnerability verification

1. Replay the normal allowed destination and capture the response without automatically following redirects. In browser-dependent flows observe the actual final origin and any user confirmation.
2. Replace only the destination with an approved controlled disallowed origin/path. Check the parsed Location or actual navigation, not the presence of the input in an error body. If arbitrary external redirects are intentionally allowed, establish a different violated security contract before treating the behavior as a flaw.
"}, {"id": 4, "text": "3. Compare the allowed destination, an invalid destination and the candidate. If a parser-boundary hypothesis exists, test one representation at a time: for example an approved network-path reference versus its absolute form. Keep the callback harmless and avoid unexpected protocols.
4. Resolve any relative Location against the effective response URL and observe each permitted hop. Server-side fetching is an SSRF question, while an anchor merely offered to a user may be a link-validation question. Do not follow to unapproved hosts or allow actual authentication artifacts into the test URL.
5. Re-run the baseline and classify whether the application reproducibly navigates to a destination prohibited by its policy. Demonstrate only that destination-control boundary unless a separately scoped consumer workflow supplies further impact evidence.

## Execution

1. Show one controlled navigation to a harmless test page identifying the destination origin, without collecting tokens, credentials or other users. For confirmation flows record the actual interaction required and whether policy intentionally permits it.
2. Remove test callback content and any stored redirect preference, restore the normal return path and close test browser sessions. Verify ordinary navigation no longer targets the test receiver.

## Analysis

1. Separate input reflection, link creation, redirect emission and actual navigation. A changed status or echoed URL alone confirms none of the latter outcomes.
"}, {"id": 5, "text": "2. Explain intentional redirectors, allowlisted partners, relative URL resolution, browser normalization, confirmation UI and intermediate trusted hops. A confirmed open redirect does not itself prove account takeover or code/token leakage; those need their own complete controlled flow.

## Evidence requirements

Preserve allowed/invalid/candidate request and response headers, destination policy, resolved scheme-host-port/path, permitted redirect chain or browser navigation, control outcomes and cleanup. Redact sensitive query values and avoid collecting them in callback logs.

## Limitations

No exhaustive URL-parser or OAuth chain testing is provided. Unknown destination policy may limit the result to observed external navigation. Third-party hops and unapproved protocols remain untested.

# Open redirect destination control

## Applicability and prerequisites

An assigned redirect, return URL or browser navigation input selects a destination. Establish the allowed destination policy and whether the feature intentionally supports arbitrary external navigation. Use controlled harmless destination URLs and stop before following to any unapproved location. Capture HTTP redirect chains and browser navigation where relevant; equivalent tooling is acceptable. Authentication codes, tokens and user data must not be sent to the receiver.

Choose only the assigned branch and obey the operation's scope, identities, rate and state-change constraints. Missing prerequisites stay explicit; a lookup signal is not proof. Equivalent available tools may replace named capabilities.

## Reconnaissance

1. Inspect the assigned return/next/location input and identify server-side Location redirects, client-side navigation or displayed links. A string echoed in a page or error does not establish navigation.
"}, {"id": 3, "text": "2. Record expected same-origin/path/partner restrictions, canonical scheme/host/port and any confirmation page. Identify whether a security workflow relies on this redirect rather than assuming phishing or token disclosure from an external link.

## Hypothesis generation

1. From recorded navigation design an allowed baseline and one controlled disallowed destination, varying only the destination interpretation. Include a nonexistent/inert input and a similarly shaped allowed destination as controls.
2. Plan a small context-justified set of URL representations such as absolute versus network-path reference, encoded delimiter or userinfo ambiguity. Define the final browser-parsed origin; do not assume a substring or visual hostname is the authority.
3. Specify whether the outcome is an HTTP redirect, a JavaScript navigation or a legitimate external link. No requests or browser navigation occur in hypothesis generation, and an unapproved token-leak chain remains outside this test.

## Vulnerability verification

1. Replay the normal allowed destination and capture the response without automatically following redirects. In browser-dependent flows observe the actual final origin and any user confirmation.
2. Replace only the destination with an approved controlled disallowed origin/path. Check the parsed Location or actual navigation, not the presence of the input in an error body. If arbitrary external redirects are intentionally allowed, establish a different violated security contract before treating the behavior as a flaw.
"}, {"id": 4, "text": "3. Compare the allowed destination, an invalid destination and the candidate. If a parser-boundary hypothesis exists, test one representation at a time: for example an approved network-path reference versus its absolute form. Keep the callback harmless and avoid unexpected protocols.
4. Resolve any relative Location against the effective response URL and observe each permitted hop. Server-side fetching is an SSRF question, while an anchor merely offered to a user may be a link-validation question. Do not follow to unapproved hosts or allow actual authentication artifacts into the test URL.
5. Re-run the baseline and classify whether the application reproducibly navigates to a destination prohibited by its policy. Demonstrate only that destination-control boundary unless a separately scoped consumer workflow supplies further impact evidence.

## Execution

1. Show one controlled navigation to a harmless test page identifying the destination origin, without collecting tokens, credentials or other users. For confirmation flows record the actual interaction required and whether policy intentionally permits it.
2. Remove test callback content and any stored redirect preference, restore the normal return path and close test browser sessions. Verify ordinary navigation no longer targets the test receiver.

## Analysis

1. Separate input reflection, link creation, redirect emission and actual navigation. A changed status or echoed URL alone confirms none of the latter outcomes.
"}, {"id": 5, "text": "2. Explain intentional redirectors, allowlisted partners, relative URL resolution, browser normalization, confirmation UI and intermediate trusted hops. A confirmed open redirect does not itself prove account takeover or code/token leakage; those need their own complete controlled flow.

Preserve allowed/invalid/candidate request and response headers, destination policy, resolved scheme-host-port/path, permitted redirect chain or browser navigation, control outcomes and cleanup. Redact sensitive query values and avoid collecting them in callback logs.

No exhaustive URL-parser or OAuth chain testing is provided. Unknown destination policy may limit the result to observed external navigation. Third-party hops and unapproved protocols remain untested.

An assigned URL, host or remote-resource input may cause server-side network requests. Establish the fetcher's intended destination, scheme, port, redirect and response-exposure policy. Use an approved controlled receiver and, for prohibited-boundary testing, an owner-designated harmless destination explicitly in assessment scope but disallowed to the feature. Permission to assess an application URL is not permission to probe its private networks. A replay client and correlated receiver or equivalent observation suffice.

2. Separate direct authority validation, redirect revalidation and DNS/address binding hypotheses. Define allowed versus forbidden destination categories and the minimal observable effect for each; do not treat every outbound public fetch as SSRF.

3. For the assigned destination rule, vary only the relevant authority/scheme/port or parser representation to the owner-designated scoped prohibited fixture. Compare the ordinary allowed destination and a nonexistent/inert destination. Do not substitute real metadata services, arbitrary private addresses or unrelated ports.
4. For redirect validation, use an allowed controlled first hop that redirects once to the approved prohibited fixture, comparing no-redirect and allowed-target redirects. Correlate each hop at controlled receivers; a redirect status returned to the user is not evidence the backend followed it.

1. Classify user-controlled input, DNS resolution, HTTP fetch, redirect following, response readability and prohibited network access separately. Callback availability alone never establishes the semantic violation.

Obtain owned test identities and policy for issuer, audience, purpose, algorithms, keys and time validity. Missing policy remains unknown. Process tokens locally with an available decoder and HTTP client; decoding never verifies a signature. Keep token/key values in sensitive internal artifacts and redact public outputs.

1. Inspect the assigned capture for where the token travels: header, cookie, URL or body. Distinguish observed authentication use from an untested assumption; a response-only token may lack an identified consumer.
2. Classify JWS, JWE, unsecured and nested forms. Read available bounded header/claim metadata, noting encrypted or inaccessible claims. Record whether key-selection fields are actually processed rather than assuming from their names. Include `alg`, `kid`, `jku`, `jwk`, `x5u`, and `x5c` only when observed or documented by the assigned flow.

## Hypothesis generation

1. Using recorded data only, choose plausible branches: integrity, bounded weak-HMAC-key assessment, algorithm/key confusion, untrusted key selection, or issuer/audience/time/purpose enforcement. Do not send requests or search keys in this context.

Remove alternate cookies/credentials and automatic refresh; compare absent, malformed and valid other-owned-identity tokens. Use a real browser and capture capability; nonbrowser replay can probe token handling but cannot by itself prove browser exploitability.

2. Identify a browser-reproducible cross-origin trigger and actual state read-back. Cross-origin and cross-site differ; record the relationship relevant to SameSite cookies rather than equating any second origin with a cross-site attacker.

## Hypothesis generation

## Vulnerability verification

# Cross-site request forgery

## Applicability and prerequisites

An assigned browser workflow changes state using credentials the browser may attach automatically. Establish the action's intended user intent/authorization policy and use an owned account with a harmless reversible setting. Know target and attacker-page origins/sites and whether the action relies on cookies or an explicitly supplied bearer credential. Use a real browser and capture capability; nonbrowser replay can probe token handling but cannot by itself prove browser exploitability.

Choose only the assigned branch and obey the operation's scope, identities, rate and state-change constraints. Missing prerequisites stay explicit; a lookup signal is not proof. Equivalent available tools may replace named capabilities.

## Reconnaissance

"}, {"id": 3, "text": "1. Inspect the assigned state-changing request for method, content type, credential transport, anti-CSRF value, Origin/Referer checks and relevant cookie attributes. An absent token is not proof; other controls or explicit user credentials may prevent forgery.
2. Identify a browser-reproducible cross-origin trigger and actual state read-back. Cross-origin and cross-site differ; record the relationship relevant to SameSite cookies rather than equating any second origin with a cross-site attacker.

## Hypothesis generation

1. Design a future normal in-site action and an attacker-page action that changes only one reversible test field. Specify how credentials would be attached without the attacker learning them, and how actual server state will be read independently.
2. Plan omitted/invalid/other-owned-session token comparisons and origin/referrer controls without assuming each missing input must be exploitable. For JSON/custom headers, include the browser preflight and whether an attacker can send an equivalent simple request.
3. For login CSRF, design an owned attacker-account login from a clean victim test browser and a final identity check; do not require an existing victim session for that branch. No live actions or forged pages are exercised during hypothesis design.

## Vulnerability verification

1. Perform the legitimate action in an owned browser session, verify the reversible field through a fresh read and restore it. Capture credentials actually used, token/session binding and request context.
"}, {"id": 4, "text": "2. With a nonbrowser client if useful, vary only token presence/value or Origin/Referer to identify a candidate acceptance condition. Use correct-session and unrelated-session controls. Label this server-side acceptance only until reproduced through the browser.
3. Serve a minimal attacker page from the approved controlled origin using a form, navigation or fetch appropriate to the actual method/content type. Do not spoof browser-forbidden headers or insert a secret token the attacker would not know. Observe preflight, redirects and actual cookie attachment.
4. Trigger the harmless test action once in the owned browser. Verify committed server state through a separate normal read, not just a success page or outbound request. Compare an invalid-token/incompatible-origin control and logged-out or credentialless behavior as relevant.
5. For login CSRF confirm whether the test browser acquired the attacker's owned identity and whether the application's login-intent policy forbids that flow. Account switching initiated normally is not the same test. Repeat a normal action and restore state after each successful variant.

## Execution

1. Demonstrate one unauthorized cross-site change to a harmless owned setting, or one owned-account login-intent effect, under realistic browser credential and request restrictions. Avoid email/password changes, purchases or notifications to others.
2. Restore the setting and original login context, remove the attacker page and end temporary sessions. Confirm that no queued request, test form or browser tab will repeat the mutation.

## Analysis

"}, {"id": 5, "text": "1. Separate a missing defense indicator, nonbrowser acceptance, browser request dispatch and committed unauthorized state. An attacker need not read the response for CSRF; inability to read it is not a refutation.
2. Explain SameSite/site relationships, preflight enforcement, explicit bearer headers, origin/referrer validation, one-time tokens, user interaction and intentional public actions. CORS governs response access and does not itself establish CSRF protection.

## Evidence requirements

Retain legitimate and forged browser requests, origin/site relationship, actual cookie/credential attachment, token provenance, preflight/redirect behavior, fresh state read-back and negative controls. Keep tokens internal and document cleanup.

# Path traversal and file inclusion boundaries

## Applicability and prerequisites

"}, {"id": 3, "text": "An assigned path, filename or template parameter selects server-side content or inclusion behavior. Establish the allowed root/resource policy and obtain an owner-provided nonsecret fixture with a known unique marker outside that allowed selector boundary, plus an allowed fixture. Use network requests to the application only; do not inspect the target filesystem, containers or source locally. If no safe prohibited fixture exists, limit testing to selector behavior and record impact as untested.

Choose only the assigned branch and obey the operation's scope, identities, rate and state-change constraints. Missing prerequisites stay explicit; a lookup signal is not proof. Equivalent available tools may replace named capabilities.

## Reconnaissance

1. Inspect assigned filename/template inputs, observed path normalization and error responses. Distinguish a resource identifier mapped by the application from a literal filesystem path; file-like parameter names alone are weak clues.
2. Identify whether the feature returns bytes, renders/includes templates or fetches remote content. A file read does not establish executable inclusion, and a remote fetch does not establish code execution. Record expected directory/type restrictions and OS/path uncertainties.

## Hypothesis generation

1. From recorded inputs design a future allowed-file baseline, a known nonexistent-path control and one boundary-crossing path targeting only the approved marker fixture. Specify the expected unique content and why access is prohibited by the selector's policy.
"}, {"id": 4, "text": "2. Plan relative segments, separator or encoding variations one at a time only where normalization clues justify them. Do not guess arbitrary system files or enumerate paths.
3. For inclusion, design a separate inert-content versus owner-approved harmless interpreted fixture comparison, if such a fixture/capability is available. Without it, leave execution unproven. No reads, uploads or remote fetches occur during hypothesis generation.

## Vulnerability verification

1. Retrieve the allowed fixture through the assigned interface and verify its unique marker. Compare the nonexistent resource and a direct ordinary application route to distinguish fallback pages, public content and path reflection.
2. Submit the smallest relative boundary-crossing selector for the approved outside fixture, keeping identity, method and other parameters fixed. Compare a path pointing to an allowed fixture and a nonexistent sibling with similar syntax.
3. If an encoding/normalization hypothesis is assigned, vary only that representation and preserve exact wire bytes. Show that returned content identifies the prohibited fixture rather than merely an error disclosing a path. Do not broaden to arbitrary traversal depths or unrelated sensitive files.
4. For local or remote inclusion, test only an owner-provided harmless fixture, with a literal-content control and a unique generated marker if interpretation is claimed. Static file bytes, a remote-host callback or an included text marker alone prove only read/fetch/inclusion, not server code execution.
"}, {"id": 5, "text": "5. Repeat the original baseline and deny/inert controls in reversed order. Confirm the exact directory/resource-policy boundary crossed and state whether the mechanism was byte retrieval, template inclusion or separately demonstrated interpretation. A readable public asset or authorized shared file is not a violation.

## Execution

1. Demonstrate only the unique nonsecret fixture bytes or owner-approved harmless inclusion marker through the affected network interface. Avoid passwords, environment files, logs, code execution payloads and remote protocol pivots.
2. Remove test fixtures through authorized owner/application procedures, restore any selector preferences and callback content, and verify ordinary allowed-file behavior. Do not delete or change preexisting target files.

## Analysis

1. Separate accepted path syntax, normalized traversal, prohibited file access and executable inclusion. Path disclosure in an error is a different narrower observation.
2. Explain aliases, symlinks, intentional shared roots, resource mapping, URL fetching, caches and fallback pages. A successful read needs policy evidence; nonownership alone does not imply denial. No result from one OS/path encoding excludes every inclusion or normalization path.

## Evidence requirements

Retain exact encoded requests, allowed/outside/nonexistent fixture markers, established allowed-root/resource policy, identity entitlement, returned bytes or generated inclusion output, repeat controls and cleanup. Use nonsecret fixtures; do not publish target filesystem details unnecessarily.

## Limitations

"}, {"id": 6, "text": "External-only access may leave actual paths, symlinks or inclusion execution unknown. Missing a scoped prohibited fixture means only tentative selector behavior can be assessed. No arbitrary local-file enumeration, log poisoning or executable inclusion chain is supplied.

Use available HTTP replay, browser or protocol capabilities appropriate to the actual channel; no
named tool is required. Preserve configured HTTP/HTTPS proxy use where the tool supports it. Work
only on the assigned interaction; this method does not authorize general discovery or new
hosts/ports.

## Accepted baselines and controls

A documented permitted field changes and can be read back independently. Record the initial value of
the candidate restricted field and the actor's actual grant to change it.

## Reconnaissance

1. Inspect the already assigned captures and contract for this method's input, identity, state and

## Hypothesis generation

1. Use recorded observations only in this section; do not send new target requests or execute the
   future tests.
2. Compare recorded request and response schemas and publicly exposed contracts. Design one-property
   future variations for server-owned fields, nested properties and operation-specific inputs. In

3. Write the expected permitted, prohibited and inconclusive outcomes and the evidence needed to

1. Repeat the ordinary update and read back its persisted value, preserving all authorization and

2. Add or modify one candidate field with an inert reversible value; keep the ordinary field and

3. Read back the candidate property through an independent authorized view or verify its specific

   insufficient.

   unauthorized binding.

## Execution

1. Apply only after the relevant boundary and operation authorization have been established. Reuse
   the validated comparison and avoid unrelated chaining or additional data collection.
2. Demonstrate one reversible prohibited field transition on a test object. If privilege or billing

1. Compare the observed result with the established policy and the local controls above. A
